Field surveys along the West African coast indicate that this species reaches a maximum total length of 30 cm [Li = 30 cm], although individuals exceeding 25 cm are uncommon in commercial catches. The estimated wet weight at birth, based upon the typical diameter of the pelagic eggs which ranges from 1 to 4 mm, is approximately 0.00032 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00032 grams]; this minute initial mass reflects the high fecundity strategy common in clupeiform fishes. In laboratory rearing experiments conducted at a stable water temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], the yolk-sac larvae completed yolk absorption and achieved first exogenous feeding after roughly 6 days [ab = roughly 6 days], a developmental rate consistent with observations in other tropical sardinella species. The brief embryonic and larval period at this thermal regime underscores the importance of warm waters for rapid early ontogeny.

Reproductive traits in Sardinella maderensis are characterized by an extended spawning season and high iteroparous output. Gravid females are known to produce between 226 and 227 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = between 226 and 227 eggs per spawning event], and the frequency of these events can reach approximately 365 spawnings per year [F_R_i = approximately 365 spawnings per year] under optimal thermal conditions of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. The estimated total length at which 50 percent of individuals attain puberty is 13.4 cm [Lp = 13.4 cm], a value derived from macroscopic gonad inspection in sampled populations. Correspondingly, the wet weight at puberty is calculated to be roughly 21.1 grams [Wwp = roughly 21.1 grams], based on the length-weight relationship established for this species along the Mauritanian shelf.

The maximum life span recorded for Madeiran sardinella is 8 years [am = 8 years] under natural environmental conditions, with this longevity estimate derived from otolith increment analysis of populations inhabiting waters at 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. This relatively extended life span for a small clupeid is consistent with a life-history strategy that balances high annual mortality from predation with sustained reproductive output over multiple seasons. The ultimate wet weight attained by adults in the wild is approximately 243 grams [Wwi = approximately 243 grams], although exceptional specimens exceeding 900 grams have been documented in the scientific literature. The asymptotic mass of 243 grams [Wwi = 243 grams] likely represents a physiological optimum in the context of the species' typical foraging environment, where zooplankton density and water temperature interact to determine growth trajectory. Comparative data from congeneric species show that Sardinella maderensis occupies an intermediate position in body size within the genus, reflecting its adaptation to specific trophic niches along the continental shelf.

Seasonal variability in oceanographic conditions exerts a strong influence on the reproductive phenology of Sardinella maderensis. Peak spawning activity coincides with the upwelling season, when nutrient-rich waters fuel abundant zooplankton blooms that provide critical food resources for both larvae and adults. The age at birth, recorded as 6 days [ab = 6 days] at 21 °C [T = 21 °C], represents a critical developmental window during which the transition from endogenous yolk reserves to exogenous feeding must occur; failure to encounter suitable prey within this timeframe leads to irreversible starvation. Field studies have shown that the species attains the length at puberty of 13.4 cm [Lp = 13.4 cm] within its first year of life in warmer, productive areas, whereas growth is more protracted in cooler peripheral regions of its distributional range. This geographic plasticity in maturation schedules is a common feature among small pelagic fishes that track environmental gradients in temperature and food availability.

Ecologically, Sardinella maderensis functions as a crucial trophic link between zooplankton production and higher-level predators such as tunas, seabirds, and marine mammals. The species' high reproductive rate, expressed through its nearly continuous spawning frequency of 365 spawnings per year [F_R_i = 365 spawnings per year] with a clutch size of 226 to 227 eggs [N_R_i = a clutch size of 226 to 227 eggs], ensures rapid population turnover and resilience to fishing pressure. The maximum longevity of 8 years [am = 8 years] under thermal conditions of 21 °C [T = 21 °C] allows multiple reproductive seasons, contributing to the species' capacity to buffer against years of poor recruitment caused by environmental stochasticity. Management strategies for this commercially important clupeid must therefore account for the biological constraints imposed by its life-history parameters, particularly the total length of 30 cm [Li = 30 cm] as a benchmark for maximum size.
